title: TEST PACK (draft): Models, data and measurable improvement
text: STEM Innovators 3.4: Illustrate how the practices of science and engineering relate to the innovation process (developing and using models; analyzing and interpreting data). STEM Innovators 3.5: Apply science and engineering practices to improve the product in a measurable manner: design, produce, test, and analyze an improved product.

items.q: Your forecaster scores 89%. A model that just says "no quake" everywhere scores 81%. What does that tell you?
c: Your model is only somewhat better than always saying no
89% means the model is nearly perfect
accuracy_only
The 81% number doesn't matter
baseline
You can't compare two models
baseline

items.q: Why does the Forecaster learn from 2016–2020 but get tested on 2021–2025?
c: To see if it works on data it never saw
Testing on the years it learned is fairer
testsame
So it can memorize the answers
testsame
The years you test on don't matter
testsame

items.q: After one change, accuracy drops from 89% to 70%, but the model now catches 109 quake areas instead of 61. How should you describe this?
c: A trade-off: more quakes caught, more false alarms
The change failed in every way
accuracy_only
Only accuracy matters, so undo it
accuracy_only
Next time, change every setting at once
onevar

items.q: You want to prove your change improved the model. What should you do?
c: Change one setting, retest, and compare to your first run
Change all the settings at once
onevar
Skip the first run and just test the new one
baseline
Test it on the years it learned from
testsame

misconceptions.accuracy_only: Accuracy alone can fool you. Also check what the model caught, what it missed, and its false alarms.
misconceptions.baseline: Always compare to a baseline, like a model that just says "no quake" everywhere. Without one, you can't tell if your model is any good.
misconceptions.testsame: A fair test uses data the model never saw. Testing on what it learned from only checks its memory.
misconceptions.onevar: Change one setting at a time. If you change several at once, you can't tell which one made the difference.
